questions.question: How do you automate REST APIs using Rest Assured?
questions.answer: REST Assured is a Java DSL that makes HTTP requests and fluent response assertions readable. I would keep the base URI and authentication in configuration, build reusable request/response specifications, create data-driven positive and negative tests, assert status, headers, schema, and business fields, and publish results in CI. I would keep API tests independent and use generated or isolated test data rather than relying on execution order. Example tradeoff: REST Assured gives strong Java/TestNG integration and reuse; Postman is faster for exploratory collaboration, while code is usually better for versioned, scalable regression suites. Do not claim a personal implementation detail unless you can support it with a real example.

questions.question: How do you validate HTTP methods and status codes?
questions.answer: I map each operation to its API contract: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes, while also checking documented idempotency and authorization. For every request I assert the expected status class and exact status where the contract requires it—for example 201 plus a Location or resource identifier after creation, 200/204 for successful updates as documented, 400 for malformed input, 401 for missing or invalid authentication, 403 for authenticated-but-forbidden access, 404 for a missing resource, 409 for a conflict, and 429 for rate limiting. I also assert the error body and headers, not just the status, because a wrong success payload can pass a shallow test.

questions.question: How do you handle OAuth2, JWT, and token refresh in API tests?
questions.answer: I separate token acquisition from business tests. A setup client obtains a token using the environment's approved grant, stores it in memory or a protected CI secret, and a request specification adds it as an Authorization Bearer header. I test missing, malformed, expired, wrong-audience, and insufficient-scope tokens, while never logging the token or secrets. For refresh, I verify the refresh-token path and retry only the intended request once after a clearly detected 401; I do not blindly retry all failures because that can hide authorization defects or duplicate non-idempotent operations. JWT tests should validate claims relevant to the contract—issuer, audience, expiry and scopes—without treating a decoded payload as proof of signature validity; signature verification belongs to the service/security test setup as appropriate.

questions.question: How do you validate responses, headers, and JSON schemas?
questions.answer: I validate at three levels: protocol (status, content type, cache and correlation headers), schema (required fields, types, enums and additional-property policy), and business behavior (values, relationships and invariants). I keep schema checks versioned with the API contract and add targeted assertions for important semantics; schema-only tests can miss a wrong ID or incorrect calculation. I also assert error schemas and content negotiation. In CI I capture a sanitized request/response correlation ID and failure diagnostics, never credentials or sensitive payloads.

questions.question: How do serialization, deserialization, and JSON parsing fit into API automation?
questions.answer: Serialization converts a typed request object into JSON; deserialization converts JSON into a typed response object. I use DTOs when the payload is stable and complex because compile-time structure and reusable builders reduce brittle string JSON. I use JsonPath for focused assertions or dynamic fields and deliberately avoid over-modeling volatile responses. The tradeoff is speed and readability versus coupling: DTOs can make schema changes fail fast, but a large model can create maintenance overhead. Regardless of technique, I still assert the wire-level status, headers, schema and key business rules; parsing successfully is not the same as correctness.

questions.question: How do you design reusable API frameworks and debug failures?
questions.answer: S: A shared API suite needs to be reusable without hiding the request details that make failures diagnosable. T: I would establish consistent configuration, authentication, data ownership, assertions, reporting and CI behavior. A: I would separate client/service methods from test intent; centralize base URI, timeouts, redaction, correlation IDs and common specs; keep schemas and test data versioned; tag smoke, contract, regression and destructive tests; and provide sanitized request/response logging on failure. For a failure, I first classify client, environment, dependency, product or test-data causes, reproduce with the exact request and correlation ID, compare the raw response with the contract, and check service logs/traces/metrics. R: I would document the root cause, add a regression test or harness improvement, and report [a concrete impact/metric only if you have one]. A framework should fail loudly on real defects, not solve instability with blanket retries.

questions.question: How would you choose between Postman and Rest Assured for a senior API-testing strategy?
questions.answer: I would use Postman for fast exploratory work, sharing examples, environment-driven manual checks and collaboration with developers or product stakeholders. I would use Rest Assured for code-reviewed, version-controlled regression and integration tests that need typed helpers, reusable fixtures, TestNG/JUnit integration and rich CI composition. They are complementary rather than mutually exclusive: a Postman collection can prove an interaction quickly, then stable checks can move into code when they need scale and maintainability. The decision depends on ownership, test volume, language/toolchain, reporting and CI needs—not on tool preference alone. Postman Collection Runner/Newman supports repeatable command-line execution, while REST Assured's Java DSL supports fluent request/response validation.

questions.question: How would you test an ad-order-management API beyond the happy path?
questions.answer: S: For an order workflow, correctness includes business rules and state transitions, not just 2xx responses. T: I would cover create, retrieve, update, submit/approve, pause and cancel paths according to the actual contract. A: I would build a matrix for required and boundary fields, invalid dates, currency/budget precision, duplicate idempotency keys, unsupported targeting, authorization by advertiser/account, conflicting state transitions, partial updates, pagination and filtering. I would verify invariants such as totals, status transitions, audit fields and no sensitive-data leakage, then test downstream dependency failure with stubs or controlled fault injection. I would use isolated data per run and correlate API assertions with logs, traces and metrics. R: I would gate releases on the contract and critical business paths, while classifying performance/load and exploratory checks separately. Replace [example rule] with a real domain rule only if known.

questions.question: Design a test strategy for an ad-order-management change. What belongs in API, UI, contract, integration, and end-to-end layers, and what runs in CI?
questions.answer: I start from risk and business invariants: order creation/editing, approval, targeting/budget validation, pacing or status transitions, permissions, and downstream delivery/reporting. Most validation goes at the API/service layer because it is fast and precise; contract tests protect producer-consumer schemas; integration tests verify queues, persistence, and external boundaries; a small UI suite proves critical user journeys and wiring. In CI I run lint/unit and API/contract tests on every change, a parallel smoke slice on deployment, and broader regression on a schedule or release gate. Tests are tagged by risk, dependency, and runtime, with quarantine requiring an owner and expiry—not silent exclusion. I would calibrate the matrix using [known risks/SLAs], not an arbitrary percentage of UI coverage.

questions.question: How would you choose among UI, API/service, and lower-level tests for an ad-order-management workflow?
questions.answer: I would test business rules at the lowest layer that gives sufficient confidence: many fast unit/component checks for budget, targeting, validation, and state transitions; service/API tests for authorization, schema, idempotency, persistence, and event contracts; and a small number of Playwright or Selenium journeys for the highest-value user paths such as create, submit, approve, and status visibility. I would use Postman/RestAssured for exploratory and API automation where appropriate and reserve UI tests for wiring and user-visible behavior. The practical pyramid advises many small fast tests, fewer coarse tests, and very few end-to-end tests, while acknowledging that exact layer names vary. Tradeoff: lower layers are fast and diagnosable but cannot prove browser integration; UI tests provide broad confidence but are slower and more failure-prone.

questions.question: How would you design a scalable, parallel-safe automation framework for UI and API tests, and what tradeoffs would you make?
questions.answer: I would separate test intent from page/API clients, centralize configuration and fixtures, use stable user-facing locators, keep tests isolated with independent browser contexts and unique data, and make API setup/cleanup explicit. In CI I would shard or use workers only after proving tests are order-independent; each worker needs isolated accounts, IDs, or namespaces, and secrets must come from the CI secret store. I would publish JUnit/HTML results, traces on first retry or failure, and logs/correlation IDs for diagnosis. Tradeoffs: more workers reduce wall-clock time but increase CPU, memory, environment contention, and data-collision risk; broad end-to-end coverage gives confidence but is slower, so fast API/component checks should cover most rules and a smaller UI layer should validate critical user journeys. I would measure [duration/flakiness/coverage] rather than assume parallelism is beneficial.

questions.question: How would you test an ad-order REST API, including status codes, auth, idempotency, and downstream correctness?
questions.answer: I define the contract first: method, URL, required headers, auth, request schema, response schema, and expected status for success and each important failure. I cover valid creation, missing or invalid fields, unauthorized and forbidden access, not-found, conflict/duplicate behavior, rate limits, and server errors without asserting unstable wording. I validate key headers, JSON schema or typed fields, and business invariants such as the order identifier, line-item totals, and state transition. For a create operation I test idempotency with the same key, verify no duplicate order, and then clean up or use isolated data. I keep tokens in CI secret storage and never print them. The tradeoff is a small fast API suite for broad contract coverage, complemented by a few UI flows that prove the user journey.

questions.question: [LinkedIn post actual] Explain your automation framework architecture. How would you structure it so it remains maintainable as an AdTech/order-management product grows?
questions.answer: I separate intent from mechanics. Tests own business assertions; workflow or service objects express reusable user journeys; page/component objects own UI locators and actions; API clients own HTTP details; and a core layer owns browser creation, fixtures, configuration, waits, reporting, and artifacts. Test data factories create unique orders, campaigns, or users through APIs where possible, while environment settings and secrets come from CI variables rather than source control. I keep page objects free of business assertions, enforce naming and review conventions, and make the smallest useful abstraction so a UI change normally affects one layer. I would validate the design with a small proof of concept, then review runtime, flake rate, and maintenance hotspots at [cadence].

T: My responsibility was to establish whether the issue was a product defect, environment problem, or test weakness, protect the release decision, and leave the suite healthier. A: I made the failure reproducible, triaged evidence with logs/traces/API data, paired with the developer or service owner, prioritized the smallest risk-reducing fix, and communicated a clear go/no-go recommendation with remaining uncertainty. I added or updated the right test at the lowest useful layer, documented ownership, and avoided masking it with an unconditional retry. R: The outcome was [verified result/metric], and the follow-up control was [dashboard, alert, review rule, or test]. I would use only facts I can substantiate from my experience.

questions.question: How do you investigate intermittent failures and distinguish a flaky test from a real product defect?
questions.answer: S/T: I would preserve every occurrence and avoid labeling it flaky just because it is intermittent. A: Correlate test result, commit, browser/container, worker, seed, test-data identifiers, timing, API status, logs, traces, and service health. Run the test repeatedly across clean workers and vary concurrency; compare the failing and passing traces. If the same product request returns an incorrect business result, it is likely a product defect; if the test's locator or shared state is nondeterministic, it is a test defect; if infrastructure is unhealthy, it is an environment issue. R: File the right defect with reproducible evidence, fix the layer that owns it, and track recurrence. For an ad-order workflow I would verify business invariants such as order status, spend/budget, targeting, and delivery events rather than only a UI assertion. Personal example: [insert your actual triage evidence].

questions.question: How would you handle shared test-data conflicts in parallel runs?
questions.answer: S/T: Parallel tests must not mutate the same logical record unless the test is explicitly about concurrency. A: Prefer factory-created, unique data per test or worker, with a correlation ID in names and metadata; seed through an API or fixture, keep immutable reference data read-only, and clean up using an idempotent API/job. Partition scarce accounts, use worker-scoped setup only when safe, and make tests order-independent. For ad-order-management data, allocate unique advertiser/campaign/order IDs and avoid asserting against globally aggregated counters while other tests write. If shared state is unavoidable, serialize only that narrow scenario and document the tradeoff. R: Parallelism becomes a speed improvement rather than a source of false failures. questions.question: What steps would you take if the automation framework suddenly failed after a deployment?
questions.answer: S/T: I would protect release decisions while quickly finding whether the break is in the product, framework, environment, or pipeline. A: Stop treating all failures as product failures; compare the last green commit and deployment, inspect dependency/browser changes, config and secrets, container image, network/authentication, and a known-good smoke test. Reproduce from the exact CI artifact, bisect the framework or application change, and use traces/logs/request IDs. If release confidence is at risk, communicate scope and evidence, use a reversible pin/rollback only with approval, and open an owner-assigned incident. R: Restore trustworthy signal first, then add a regression check and remove any temporary pin. Personal example: [insert a real framework or pipeline incident and your communication path].

questions.question: Which quality signals would you put on a CI dashboard, and why is pass rate alone insufficient?
questions.answer: I would separate product quality from test-health and delivery signals: escaped defects by severity, critical-path scenario coverage, contract/API failure rate, defect reopen rate, change-failure or rollback rate, and business invariants such as order submission correctness; plus test pass rate, first-attempt pass rate, flake rate, retry rate, duration, queue time, quarantined tests, and artifact completeness. I would segment by suite, browser, service, commit, and environment rather than average everything together. Observability adds user-centered SLIs/SLOs and traces/metrics/logs for production behavior. Pass rate can be green while tests are being retried, skipped, quarantined, or asserting weakly. Tradeoff: fewer high-value signals with owners beat a vanity dashboard of dozens of unacted metrics.

A: I quantified occurrences using the available CI history, grouped failures by symptom and environment, reproduced the smallest case, and partnered with the relevant developer/platform owner. I would fix synchronization or isolation, improve test-data setup, add trace/log/request-ID collection, and document an owner, exit criteria, and review date for any quarantine. I would communicate the impact and decision clearly in the PR or incident record. R: [Insert your actual outcome—such as lower recurrence, faster diagnosis, or a removed quarantine—without inventing a number]. The principle is to leave the suite more diagnosable and maintainable, not merely green today.

questions.answer: S: A release discussion involved a defect whose customer, revenue, targeting, or order-state impact was not yet agreed. T: I owned making the risk visible and helping the team reach a release decision. A: I reproduced the issue, documented expected versus actual behavior, identified affected flows and data conditions, and separated facts from assumptions. I proposed options—fix now, mitigate and monitor, or defer with an explicit risk owner—and asked product/development to confirm business impact. R: We made a traceable decision based on severity, exposure, workaround, and rollback/monitoring readiness. questions.question: As QA Lead, how would you take ownership when an escaped production defect is reported?
questions.answer: S: A production defect has escaped and may affect ad creation, order approval, billing, targeting, or delivery. T: I would protect customers and restore confidence while finding the systemic cause, not merely assigning blame. A: I would confirm scope and severity from logs, traces, requests, and a minimal reproduction; coordinate containment such as rollback, feature flag, or operational workaround; and establish a single incident owner and update cadence. Then I would add the missing test at the right layer, check whether similar paths are vulnerable, review the requirement and test-data assumptions, and track prevention actions to closure. R: The result should be a documented impact/containment decision, verified fix, regression coverage, and a blameless learning record. questions.question: How do Cucumber hooks, tags, and Scenario Outline fit together, and what would you keep out of hooks?
questions.answer: Step definitions map Gherkin steps to code. A Scenario Outline runs the same scenario for each Examples row, which is useful for a small, readable data set. Tags organize and select scenarios and can restrict conditional hooks. Before and After hooks are appropriate for low-level setup and teardown such as starting a browser, isolating data, and attaching a screenshot on failure. I keep business setup visible in Background or steps when a non-technical reader needs to understand it, because hidden hooks reduce feature readability. I also avoid global mutable state and make each scenario independent so tags and parallel execution do not change its meaning. The tradeoff is fewer duplicated steps versus avoiding giant outlines that become a data-driven programming language.

questions.answer: I use a frequency map, then a second pass so output order follows the original array. This is O(n) time and O(n) additional space. I would clarify whether the interviewer wants each duplicate once or every repeated occurrence; this implementation returns each value once. For objects, I would use a stable key or domain identifier rather than Set's reference identity.

questions.question: Write Java logic to find duplicate elements in an integer array, and state its complexity.
questions.answer: Use a HashSet for values already seen and a second insertion-ordered set for duplicates. This is O(n) expected time and O(n) additional space. If sorted output is required, sort first for O(n log n), or use a TreeSet at an O(log n) per-insert cost. I would clarify whether duplicate values should be reported once and whether order matters.
